clue.text: Bill gets Paul awfully firm in Mexico

definitions.note: a place in Mexico, a noun phrase by way of 'in'

parts.note: ac is the abbreviation for account, a bill

indicators.note: awfully means badly done, so the letters of the name are badly arranged

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
Co is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: Bill and Paul run into trouble with a company in Mexico.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill and Paul look like two men; Bill is an account.
explanation.definitionFit: Acapulco is a Pacific resort city in the Mexican state of Guerrero.

clue.text: Shagged-out feeling of high-flier let loose in fast car?

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the car

parts.note: Jag is short for a Jaguar, a fast British car

indicators.note: let loose means set free and scattered, so those letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A high-flier let loose in a sports car ends up exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: Shagged-out is British slang for exhausted; the high-flier is literally someone travelling by air.
explanation.definitionFit: Jet lag is the tiredness that air travellers feel after crossing time zones.

clue.text: Our mag's reported pros

indicators.note: reported means passed on by word of mouth, so it is the sound that counts

parts.note: our magazine is Private Eye, here as the plural Eyes

explanation.surface: Our magazine's own reporting reveals that professionals were involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our mag' is Private Eye, which runs this crossword. 'Pros' looks like professionals; it means votes for.
explanation.definitionFit: Ayes are votes in favour, the pros in a contest of pros and cons.

clue.text: Provincial arse turned pink

parts.note: bum is British slang for the backside

indicators.note: turned means twisted round, so the colour word's letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A country type's bottom has gone pink.
explanation.definitionFit: A bumpkin is an unsophisticated person from the countryside, and provincial as a noun means someone from outside the capital.

clue.text: Stuffing rounded plug in coat

indicators.note: rounded suggests things moved round, so the following letters circulate into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Padding a coat with a round plug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuffing' suggests padding or upholstery; it is crude slang for having sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuffing is vulgar British slang for having sex, which is a synonym of mating.

clue.text: The last men's bollocks

definitions.meaning: first meaning: shoemakers, who shape shoes on a last
second meaning: rhyming slang for nonsense

explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' looks like final; a last is a foot-shaped block used in shoemaking. Cobblers is British rhyming slang meaning rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoe repairers work on lasts, and the trade's name is also slang for nonsense via the rhyme awls and balls.

clue.text: What fags might end up in — not hard to get off the straight and narrow

indicators.note: not says the following letter is absent from the word

parts.words: What fags might end up in
parts.note: fags is British slang for cigarettes, whose ends finish in this dish
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Where cigarette ends go, and how to stray from virtue without much effort.
explanation.walkthrough: Fags is British slang for cigarettes, not the slur it might seem.
explanation.definitionFit: To go astray is to wander from the right path, morally or literally, which is leaving the straight and narrow.

clue.text: Queer circle at university get lost

parts.note: screwy is slang for odd or peculiar
a circle is shaped like the letter O
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: An odd little clique at college is told to clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queer' here means strange, not the noun it seems to be in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are rude imperatives telling someone to go away, so the phrase and the curse are interchangeable.

clue.text: Windy type, one into kinky boots

indicators.note: one thing going into another puts it inside, so the single letter sits within the rest
kinky means twisted or bent, so the letters of the boots are bent out of order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A flatulent person has a fetish for kinky boots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Windy type' suggests someone who breaks wind; it is really a player of a wind instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: An oboe is a woodwind instrument, so its player is a musician who works with wind.

clue.text: Foreign bodies increasingly found in British bathrooms?

definitions.text: Foreign bodies increasingly found in British bathrooms?

parts.words: Foreign bodies increasingly found in British bathrooms?
parts.note: surface reading: alien objects or contaminants turning up in British washrooms more and more
setter's reading: people from abroad, specifically tradesmen from an Eastern European country who fit and repair bathrooms

explanation.walkthrough: 'Foreign bodies' suggests dirt or debris; read literally it means workers from overseas. It refers to the 2000s stereotype of the Polish plumber after EU enlargement.
explanation.definitionFit: After 2004 many tradesmen from Poland worked in Britain, so foreign workers fitting British bathrooms became a widely noted trend.

clue.text: Good to get away from Glenda's coarse material

indicators.note: something getting away leaves the word it was in, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: Glenda Slagg is the spoof columnist in Private Eye, where this puzzle appears
G is the usual abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Something good escapes the vulgar writing of a gossip columnist.
explanation.walkthrough: Glenda Slagg is Private Eye's parody of Fleet Street women columnists; one of the two final Gs goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Slag is the rough, glassy waste left over when metal is smelted from ore.

clue.text: A dick's an amusing and informative organ!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: dick is slang for a detective, especially one hired privately
second meaning: the satirical magazine that publishes this crossword, an organ being a periodical

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dick' and 'organ' together suggest an anatomical joke; dick means detective and organ means publication.
explanation.definitionFit: A hired investigator is called this, and it is also the name of the British satirical fortnightly where this puzzle runs.

clue.text: Worsted clad police — not such a bad thing

indicators.note: worsted means beaten or defeated, so the letters are knocked about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Police dressed in woollen worsted cloth — no great sin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worsted' suggests a woollen fabric; it means beaten.
explanation.definitionFit: A peccadillo is a minor sin or trivial fault, an offence that is not very serious.

clue.text: Is able to go arse over tip after cold drink

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

indicators.note: going arse over tip means tumbling head over heels, so the words are turned end to end

parts.note: can means is able
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone takes a tumble after a cold drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a drunk falling over; the second half is read backwards and placed after the cold letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cognac is a brandy from the French region of the same name, so it is a type of alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Finds small faults in grooms like apes?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: quibbles over trivial errors
second meaning: literally plucks lice eggs from a companion's fur

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grooms' suggests bridegrooms being criticised; it is the verb for cleaning fur.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb for fussy fault-finding comes from primates removing lice eggs from one another while grooming.

clue.text: Slight tossing until grabbing Sonya's top

indicators.note: grabbing takes hold of something, so the jumbled word wraps around the selected letter
tossing throws things about, so the following word's letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

indicators.note: the top of a word is its beginning, so only the opening letter of the name is used

parts.note: the first letter of the name Sonya

explanation.surface: A slender figure is tossing about until she grabs Sonya's top off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' looks like an adjective meaning slim; it is a noun meaning a snub.
explanation.definitionFit: A slight is a snub or affront, so it means an act of disrespect.

clue.text: Charity's crap legs and arse

indicators.note: crap means badly made or shoddy, so the letters come out in a poor arrangement

parts.note: the two body words, taken as written; and joins them

explanation.surface: A woman called Charity has awful legs and backside.
explanation.walkthrough: Charity reads as a woman's name; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Largesse is generosity in giving money or gifts, a close synonym of charity.

clue.text: Curtailed prison sentence given to Archer type when the rocket goes up?

definitions.note: the noun for the moment of launch, defined by when it happens

indicators.note: curtailed means cut short at the end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a life sentence, the longest prison term
Jeffrey Archer, a novelist and Tory peer, is the type of an upper-class toff

explanation.surface: Jeffrey Archer, jailed in 2001 for perjury, gets a reduced sentence just as a rocket launches.
explanation.walkthrough: Archer is not a bowman but Lord Archer; a toff is a posh British upper-class person.
explanation.definitionFit: Lift-off is the moment a rocket leaves the launch pad and rises.

clue.text: Removing the nuts from actors group, before making judgement

indicators.note: before says the first piece is placed ahead of the second in the answer

parts.note: the cast is the group of actors in a production
rating something is making a judgement of it

explanation.surface: Something removing the nuts from a group of actors before a judgement is made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' suggests the mad members of a troupe; it is slang for testicles.
explanation.definitionFit: Castrating means removing the testicles, for which nuts is a crude slang word.

clue.text: Claim climber's into lap dancing

indicators.note: going into something puts it inside, so the plant sits within the other letters
dancing moves things around, so the letters of lap swap places

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
the pea is a climbing plant; the 's means is

explanation.surface: A mountaineer gets into lap dancing and makes a claim about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The climber is a plant, not a mountaineer.
explanation.definitionFit: An appeal is a formal request or claim, as in an appeal for compensation.

clue.text: The party of Blair, 'Right' rather than 'New'

indicators.note: rather than means one thing stands in place of another, so the abbreviation for right takes the place of the one for new

parts.note: Tony Blair, Labour Prime Minister 1997 to 2007
N is the abbreviation for new
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Blair's party is now more right-wing than New Labour.
explanation.walkthrough: The jibe is that Blair's New Labour was really Conservative; swapping N for R in his first name makes the point.
explanation.definitionFit: Tory is the common name for Britain's Conservative Party, a political party.

clue.text: Empty Tory bluster from a bullying leader

indicators.note: emptying a word takes out its inside, leaving only its outermost letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of Tory
to rant is to bluster loudly

explanation.surface: Hollow Conservative bluster coming from an overbearing leader.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyrant is a cruel, oppressive ruler, so a leader who bullies.

clue.text: An annoying thing that's said to make you glass-bottomed?

indicators.note: said tells us the phrase works by how it sounds when spoken, not how it is written

parts.note: a sheet of glass fitted in your backside would make you glass-bottomed

explanation.surface: A daft question about what nuisance could give you a glass behind.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for a nuisance sounds exactly like a window pane lodged in your rear.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is crude British slang for an irritating person or thing, a nuisance.

clue.text: Something with which to break into (being topless) showbiz award

indicators.note: topless means without its top, so the first letter of the tool is removed

parts.words: Something with which to break into
parts.note: a jemmy is a burglar's crowbar

explanation.surface: How a topless performer might break into showbiz and win an award.
explanation.walkthrough: Topless suggests nudity; it means the first letter is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: The Emmy is the main American television industry award, a showbusiness prize.

clue.text: Straw poll's last to include one — that's a beast

indicators.note: including something holds it inside, so the joined pieces wrap around the single letter

parts.note: Jack Straw was a Labour cabinet minister

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept from the word poll

parts.note: the final letter of poll
a means one, as in a single thing

explanation.surface: Jack Straw's showing in the latest poll proves he is an animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Straw poll' looks like a phrase; Straw is the British politician Jack Straw, Foreign Secretary in Blair's government.
explanation.definitionFit: A jackal is a wild dog of Africa and Asia, so it is an animal.

clue.text: Iron skirt to get a good bloke? Not she!

definitions.note: a jokey definition: the person who would not answer to the female pronoun in the sense meant, i.e. not a woman content to dress up for a man

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
a mini is a very short skirt
a saint is a good man, abbreviated St

explanation.surface: Should a woman iron her skirt to land a decent man? She would refuse.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a joke: the kind of woman who would never put on a miniskirt to catch a man. 'Iron' looks like a verb; it is the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A campaigner for women's equality would reject the idea of dressing up to win a husband, so she is the one who says no.
